text: Flow Designer versus the legacy Workflow Editor. Before you build your first flow, you need to know where ServiceNow's automation tooling came from, why two tools still exist side by side today, and which one this entire course is actually going to teach you.

The Workflow Editor, built on the wf_workflow table, was ServiceNow's original automation canvas. You wire together activities — a Generate Approval, a Run Script, an Update Field — connected by lines showing execution order. It's powerful, but genuinely developer-oriented: activities often need JavaScript, and the canvas gets visually tangled fast once you add more than a few branches. Reading one means tracing lines across the screen.

Flow Designer, built on sys_hub_flow, is the modern replacement ServiceNow has promoted since roughly the Kingston and London releases. A flow reads top to bottom: one trigger, then a linear sequence of actions, with if/else branches and loops shown as clearly labeled blocks instead of crossing lines. Most configuration happens through dropdowns and data pills, not script fields.

ServiceNow hasn't removed the Workflow Editor, and it won't force existing Workflows to migrate — that risks breaking production automation across thousands of instances. So both tools coexist: legacy Workflows keep running as built, while Flow Designer is where all new automation gets built. That leaves you two real skills — building new flows, and reading an existing legacy Workflow well enough not to break it.

This course teaches Flow Designer exclusively for building — you won't construct a single legacy Workflow here. Next up: the three building blocks inside every flow — flows, actions, and subflows, and how they fit together.
